text.title: Code Review Cycle Core Rules
text.summary: 5 testable rules every Code Review Cycle application must enforce. These are HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them. Folds in the former principles file: Review type taxonomy, three AI assistance levels, multi-model strategy, and AI tool landscape for 2026.

rule.statement: Review MUST run 3 steps (pre-screen → parallel reviewers → merge); skipping the merge is rejected.
Every finding MUST carry severity ∈ {BLOCK, WARN, NOTE} + cited line + suggested fix.
rule.rationale: Free-text findings can't be prioritised or auto-actioned.

rule.statement: Every BLOCK finding MUST be addressed by a human before merge; AI cannot self-clear BLOCKs.
rule.rationale: AI clearing its own blocks is the rubber-stamp anti-pattern.

rule.statement: Merge step MUST writeback novel patterns to patterns.md and novel mistakes to mistakes.md. The review cycle is not complete until patterns.md is updated with learnings from the review.
rule.rationale: Findings without writeback recur. Post-merge reflexion is the most frequently skipped step. If skipped, the same issues recur in subsequent tasks because they never enter the project's pattern memory.

rule.statement: Business-logic and security-context judgement MUST be human; AI advises only.
Use AI pre-screening (Level 1) on every PR before human review; use AI co-review (Level 2) for complex changes; use AI validation (Level 3) after human approval for safety-critical code.
rule.rationale: Level 1 cleans up noise before human review, reducing review fatigue. Level 2 augments humans with explanations and pattern references. Level 3 provides final safety net. All three require human oversight — AI review without human review increases change failure rates 30%. The three levels are itemised in the section below.

rule.statement: Use a different model for review than the model that generated the code.
rule.rationale: The model that wrote the code has systematic blind spots for its own output. A separate review model catches different failure modes and provides genuine checks-and-balances. Step 2 of `content/04-procedure.xml` runs the cross-model reviewer.

rule.statement: Treat AI review findings as suggestions for humans to consider, not hard gates.
rule.rationale: AI reviewers miss: business logic (no domain understanding), security implications (flags patterns, misses context), architecture decisions (no system-wide view), edge cases (misses what it has not seen), performance at scale (does not know load patterns). r3-human-on-block is the one exception: a BLOCK is a gate, but a human clears it.

rule.statement: Every SDD task must pass two explicit quality checkpoints before marking done: self-review and PR review.
rule.rationale: Checkpoints make quality gates explicit and verifiable, preventing the "it works on my machine" failure mode common in AI-assisted development. The checkpoint block is shown in `content/05-examples.xml`.

rule.statement: After every PR merge, run a reflexion step: record what review patterns caught issues and what AI missed that humans found.
rule.rationale: Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) demonstrates that verbal reinforcement from retained review examples measurably improves agent reliability on subsequent similar code. Skipping reflexion means each task starts with zero learning from prior reviews. r4-reflexion-writeback names the files; this rule names the questions.

section.title: Review types
section.p: Reviews are classified by reviewer and by focus area. AI assistance effectiveness varies significantly by focus area.

list.item: Self-review (author): completeness, obvious issues — before PR creation
AI pre-review (LLM): style, patterns, missing tests, security red flags — on PR creation
Automated (CI/CD): tests, lint, security scans — on PR creation
Peer review (team member): logic, design, patterns — after automated checks pass
Architectural review (senior/lead): system design, consistency — for complex changes
Security review (security team): vulnerabilities, auth/authz — for sensitive code
High AI effectiveness: readability, security pattern matching, style compliance
Medium AI effectiveness: performance pattern detection, test coverage metrics
Low AI effectiveness: business logic correctness, architecture decisions, edge cases
Level 1 (AI pre-screen): style compliance, common anti-patterns, missing tests, doc gaps, security red flags — runs before human sees the PR
Level 2 (AI co-reviewer): inline comments during human review — explains complex code, suggests alternatives, highlights similar codebase patterns
Level 3 (AI validation): post-human-approval — security scans, integration checks, AC verification against design doc
CodeRabbit: structured PR review with 40+ linters
